title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Head-to-Toe Assessment—Sequence, Techniques & Documentation
html:
A head-to-toe assessment is a systematic examination that establishes a current baseline, detects change, and guides focused follow-up. It is not a ritual that must continue while a client is deteriorating. The RN first confirms immediate stability, then combines the health history, general survey, physical findings, devices, trends, and client concerns into one clinical picture.

Learning goals

  • Prepare the client, environment, and equipment for a safe and respectful assessment.
  • Use inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation correctly.
  • Complete a consistent head-to-toe sequence while adapting to acuity and client needs.
  • Compare bilateral findings and current data with the client’s baseline.
  • Recognize findings that require a focused assessment or urgent escalation.
  • Document objective findings, actions, communication, and response.

Begin with safety, consent, and context

Review the reason for care, current concerns, relevant history, orders, precautions, recent vital signs, pain, mobility risk, and lines or devices. Gather needed equipment so the client is not repeatedly exposed or repositioned. Perform hand hygiene, clean shared equipment according to policy, use appropriate personal protective equipment, and verify the client with two approved identifiers.

Introduce your name and role, explain what the examination involves, ask permission before touch, and protect privacy. Ask how the client prefers to be addressed and whether anyone present may remain. Use a qualified interpreter when needed. Expose only the area being examined, restore clothing or linens promptly, and offer a chaperone according to client preference and organizational policy. Explain sensitive examinations separately; perform them only when clinically indicated, authorized, and within scope.

Stability comes before the routine sequence

Observe the client from the doorway and during conversation. Note appearance, position, work of breathing, skin color, responsiveness, speech, movement, distress, and equipment. Complete an immediate primary survey of airway, breathing, circulation, and mental status. If the client has severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, new unresponsiveness, uncontrolled bleeding, or another sign of instability, stop the routine assessment, protect the client, obtain assistance, and initiate the appropriate emergency response.

A checklist does not outrank acuity
A complete examination supports care only when the client is stable enough for it. An unexpected cue may require the RN to change position, obtain vital signs, begin a focused assessment, call for help, or activate an emergency pathway before completing the remaining systems.

Use the four core techniques

  • Inspection: deliberately observe color, shape, symmetry, movement, behavior, devices, drainage, and the surrounding environment. Adequate light and exposure are essential.
  • Palpation: use touch to assess temperature, moisture, texture, tenderness, pulses, edema, position, or masses as appropriate. Warm the hands, begin gently, and leave a painful area until last when the client is stable.
  • Percussion: tap the body surface to help estimate underlying density, borders, or tenderness when this technique is indicated and within the examination being performed.
  • Auscultation: listen directly on the skin in a quiet environment. Use the diaphragm or bell as appropriate and compare expected landmarks systematically.

For most systems, inspection precedes palpation, percussion, and auscultation. The abdomen is the important sequence exception: inspect, auscultate, then percuss and palpate. Touching or percussing first can change bowel activity and reduce the validity of the finding. If abdominal pain is present, assess the painful area last unless urgent instability changes priorities.

Use a reproducible head-to-toe flow

A consistent sequence decreases omissions, but the exact order may be adapted to the setting, client position, developmental needs, isolation requirements, comfort, and acuity. One practical inpatient flow is:

  1. General survey and measurements: appearance, behavior, distress, mobility, communication, hydration and nutrition cues, pain, vital signs, oxygen delivery, height or weight when indicated.
  2. Mental and neurologic screen: level of consciousness, orientation or baseline cognition, speech, pupils when indicated, facial symmetry, movement, strength, sensation, and changes from baseline.
  3. Head, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and neck: vision or hearing aids, oral mucosa and swallowing cues, tracheal alignment, neck movement, and other focused findings.
  4. Respiratory: rate, rhythm, depth, effort, symmetry, cough, oxygen device and settings, skin effects, and anterior and posterior lung sounds.
  5. Cardiovascular and peripheral perfusion: heart rate and rhythm, relevant heart sounds, skin color and temperature, capillary refill, edema, and peripheral pulses.
  6. Abdomen and elimination: symptoms, contour and symmetry, bowel sounds before percussion or palpation, tenderness, intake and output, and urinary or bowel pattern.
  7. Musculoskeletal and function: alignment, range of motion, strength, gait or transfer ability, assistive devices, and fall risk.
  8. Skin and pressure areas: color, moisture, temperature, integrity, pressure points, wounds, dressings, and device-related pressure.
  9. Lines, tubes, drains, and access sites: indication, placement or securement, surrounding tissue, patency or output as applicable, prescribed settings, and ongoing need.

Cluster the examination to reduce unnecessary movement. For example, assess posterior lungs, spine, sacrum, and posterior skin while the client is safely turned. Return the bed to a safe position, place needed items and the call system within reach, and perform hand hygiene when finished.

Compare sides, landmarks, and time

Compare corresponding right and left landmarks when symmetry is expected: breath sounds, chest movement, pulses, strength, sensation, temperature, edema, and range of motion. Move side to side at the same level rather than finishing every point on one side first. Never palpate both carotid arteries simultaneously because this can reduce cerebral blood flow.

“Within expected range” depends on the client, context, and reliable baseline—not on an assumption that a finding is normal for age or diagnosis. Ask whether asymmetry or limitation is new. Compare with prior documentation, vital-sign trends, medication timing, recent procedures, oxygen requirements, intake and output, laboratory results, and the client’s report. Validate an unexpected measurement or technique problem when the client is stable, but do not delay action for a clearly dangerous finding.

Turn unexpected findings into clinical decisions

When a new cue appears, assess it rather than merely recording it. Confirm the finding when appropriate, obtain relevant measurements, perform a focused assessment, compare with baseline, and look for related cues. Prioritize urgency by airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic change, severity, rate of change, and potential harm. Initiate permitted safety actions, communicate through the appropriate pathway, and evaluate the response.

Examples include new unilateral weakness, unequal pupils, a cool pulseless extremity, new crackles with increasing oxygen need, chest pressure, rapidly expanding edema, abdominal rigidity, fresh bleeding, or a newly confused client. A normal finding in another system does not cancel a time-sensitive cue.

Respect delegation boundaries

Assistive personnel may collect selected routine data when the client is stable and organizational policy permits. The RN remains responsible for deciding what assessment is required, validating concerning or inconsistent data, interpreting the pattern, completing focused nursing assessments, initiating nursing actions, communicating changes, and evaluating outcomes. “The assistant already checked” is not a substitute for RN follow-up when risk is present.

Document a usable clinical picture

Chart promptly and objectively. Include the assessment time and relevant conditions; location and laterality; measurements; device, oxygen, or position details; comparison with baseline; associated symptoms; focused follow-up; interventions; whom you notified and when; orders or actions received; and the client’s response. Use approved terminology and avoid labels such as “normal,” “good,” or “looks bad” when specific findings are available.

For example: “0940: New left facial droop and left arm drift; speech slurred; last observed at baseline 0915. Airway patent, respirations unlabored, point-of-care glucose obtained per protocol. Emergency response activated at 0942; client remained in bed with RN present.” This record preserves the cue, timing, assessment, action, and safety response without assigning an independent medical diagnosis.

Clinical example

During a routine morning assessment, an RN observes that a client now pauses after three words and uses accessory muscles. The RN stops the planned head-to-toe sequence, positions the client to support breathing, assesses airway, respiratory rate and effort, oxygen saturation and prescribed oxygen delivery, auscultates lung sounds, obtains assistance, and communicates the change from baseline. After ordered interventions, the RN reassesses work of breathing, oxygenation, mental status, and the client’s response before deciding whether the remainder of the examination is appropriate.
